notation.meaning: Any function of the two variables
Average of $Y$ for a given value of $X$
Original and new variable of integration

blocks.md: A double integral adds up something over an area rather than along a line — total probability over all combinations of two variables, for example. Fubini's theorem says you can do it in two steps, one variable at a time, and in either order. That is exactly how you get the distribution of one variable from a joint distribution: integrate the other one out. It also makes the proof of the law of iterated expectations short.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is the working tool for any calculation involving two random variables together, from covariances to conditional expectations.
**Fubini's theorem**: if $\iint|f|\,dA < \infty$, the order of integration does not matter. For non-rectangular regions, the inner limits depend on the outer variable.

- Marginal: $f_X(x) = \int f(x,y)\,dy$ — integrate out the other variable
- Conditional: $f(y\mid x) = f(x,y)/f_X(x)$
- Expectation: $E[g(X,Y)] = \iint g(x,y)f(x,y)\,dy\,dx$
$f(x,y) = x + y$ on the unit square. It is a valid density: $\iint (x+y)\,dA = 1$. Marginal: $f_X(x) = x + \tfrac12$. Mean: $E[X] = \int_0^1 x(x + \tfrac12)\,dx = 7/12 \approx 0.583$.

sections.heading: The law of iterated expectations, proved

blocks.tex: E\big[E[Y\mid X]\big] = \int\left(\int y\,f(y\mid x)\,dy\right)f_X(x)\,dx = \iint y\,f(x,y)\,dy\,dx = E[Y]

blocks.md: The middle step uses $f(y\mid x)f_X(x) = f(x,y)$; the last uses Fubini to integrate out $x$ first.

- Wrong inner limits on a non-rectangular region (e.g. the triangle $0 \leq y \leq x \leq 1$).
- Swapping the order for an integrand that is not absolutely integrable.

- **Probability / econometrics**: continuous-variable proofs of the [Law of Iterated Expectations](note:law-of-iterated-expectations) and [Law of Total Variance](note:law-of-total-variance); covariances; the conditional mean in [Conditional Mean vs Linear Projection](note:conditional-mean-vs-linear-projection).
- **Inequality**: integrating a joint distribution of income and group to get [Within- and Between-Group Inequality](note:within-and-between-group-inequality) components.
